title: Local opposition to AI data centers crosses party lines because communities separate national technological ambition from who pays local costs
source_unit: University of Massachusetts Amherst Poll, September 2026 national public-opinion poll on AI data centers and presidential AI handling
geography: United States; national adult sample fielded August 21-26, 2026

observations.period: August 21-26, 2026; local consent and cross-partisan opposition

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the UMass Amherst national poll

local_data_center_support.unit: percent supporting construction of an AI data center in their local community

local_data_center_opposition.unit: percent opposing construction of an AI data center in their local community

democratic_opposition.unit: percent of Democrats opposing local AI data-center construction

republican_opposition.unit: percent of Republicans opposing local AI data-center construction

cross_party_route.value: Local siting opposition is substantially broader than a simple partisan rejection of AI or a national technology agenda.

observations.method: UMass Poll national survey of 1,000 respondents, matched and weighted to an ACS-based sampling frame on demographic and political variables; reported margin of error 3.5%.
observations.uncertainty: This is a cross-sectional opinion survey and a hypothetical local-siting question; it does not measure actual project votes, permitting outcomes, or realized local effects.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults by party, ideology, age, gender, education, income, race, 2024 vote, and movement-affiliation measures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Opposition may reflect general local-development resistance, prior infrastructure experiences, or question framing rather than a stable view of all AI data centers.

observations.period: August 2026; open-ended reasons for local opposition

denominator.unit: U.S. adults; each open-ended response assigned one substantive or residual theme

environmental_resource_harm.unit: percent of responses coded as environmental harm or depletion of natural resources

local_disruption_land_use.unit: percent coded as local disruption, land use, or poor community fit

utility_cost_burden.unit: percent coded as higher utility bills or economic burden on residents

ai_industry_distrust.unit: percent coded as rejection of AI or distrust of the AI industry

local_cost_mechanism.value: Most coded opposition centered on tangible local resource and community costs rather than generalized opposition to generative AI.

observations.method: UMass Poll inductive thematic coding of open-ended answers; each response assigned to one of five substantive themes or a residual category.
observations.uncertainty: The coding is publisher-reported and not an independent qualitative audit; one-theme assignment compresses mixed motives, and percentages describe responses rather than population-level causal prevalence.
observations.subgroup: All 1,000 respondents who answered the open-ended local data-center question; valence is associated with coded themes in the release.
observations.counterinterpretation: Respondents may use local environmental language to express broader distrust of corporate development or political decision-making; open-ended answers do not reveal which concern would change a permitting decision.

observations.period: August 2026; local cost-benefit conflict and strategic competitiveness

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the national poll

economic_benefit_support_theme.unit: percent of open-ended responses coded as economic benefits, technological necessity, or competitiveness

local_benefit_argument.value: Supporters cite jobs, tax revenue, business investment, and local economic development.

strategic_competitiveness_argument.value: Some supporters frame data centers as necessary for U.S. economic dominance and competition with China.

cost_benefit_split.value: The siting debate separates broad national technological benefits from concentrated local resource, utility, land-use, and quality-of-life costs.

observations.method: Descriptive synthesis of open-ended responses and subgroup support/opposition results.
observations.uncertainty: The study does not estimate the actual distribution of data-center benefits and costs, nor test whether community-benefit agreements or rate protections alter opinion.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, including partisan and ideological subgroups; supporter explanations are a minority-coded response group.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strategic-competition arguments may coexist with local protections if residents believe benefits are fairly shared; opposition does not imply rejection of AI development elsewhere.

observations.period: March-August 2026 comparison; political accountability for AI

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the August 2026 UMass Poll; comparison with March 2026 reported by the poll

presidential_ai_handling_poor.unit: percent saying President Trump has handled artificial intelligence poorly in August 2026

presidential_ai_handling_well.unit: percent saying President Trump has handled artificial intelligence well in August 2026

not_well_at_all_change.value: The share saying AI was handled not well at all rose from 36% in March to 43% in August.

issue_accountability_route.value: AI infrastructure and policy are becoming a political performance test, not only a technology-adoption question.

observations.method: UMass Poll repeated cross-sectional comparison of presidential handling of AI; August sample was 1,000 adults and the release reports March comparison figures.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison is not a panel estimate and cannot isolate data-center opinion, specific events, or partisan changes as causes of the shift.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults with party, ideology, age, gender, and other subgroup comparisons reported in the poll tables.
observations.counterinterpretation: Issue approval may track broader presidential approval or current events rather than a distinct judgment about AI infrastructure policy.

related_sources.claim: The official UMass Poll page provides sample, weighting, margin of error, local data-center support/opposition, open-ended thematic coding, and presidential AI-handling results.

boundary: This record adds a local-consent and political-accountability route: opposition to AI data centers crosses party lines because residents distinguish national technological benefits from concentrated local costs and community fit. It does not establish realized environmental harm, utility-rate causality, permitting behavior, project economics, or causal presidential approval effects.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official UMass Poll report page was reviewed for methodology, local support/opposition, party comparisons, open-ended thematic coding, supporter arguments, and repeated presidential AI-handling estimates.
